CHAPTER E1.3 · ELECTIVE 1

CHAPTER E1.3 · ELECTIVE 1 · FEBRUARY

Distances, prisms and pyramids

How far is a lamp from the sloping roof surface? How tall is a pyramid whose base lies at a slant in space? How much glass does a glass pyramid need, how much air is inside? With the foot of the perpendicular and the Hesse normal form you calculate distances of points, lines and planes to planes, and with the cross product the surface areas and volumes of solids whose corners are only given as coordinates.

7 LESSONS2 UNITSREAL 3D
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • find the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a plane
  • calculate distances point–plane, line–plane and plane–plane
  • calculate surface areas of prisms and pyramids with the cross product
  • find volumes from the base and the height, even if the height is a distance to a slanted plane

$\tfrac{6}{3} = 2$

Volume of a pyramid with base area 16 and height 6?

$\tfrac13 \cdot 16 \cdot 6 = 32$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Distances of points, lines and planes to planes

The distance between two points is the length of their connecting vector. The question of how far a point $P$ is from a plane is harder: the plane has infinitely many points. The nearest one is the foot of the perpendicular $F$, because the shortest connection is perpendicular to the plane, so it runs in the direction of the normal vector.

You set up the perpendicular line through $P$ with the direction vector $\vec n$ and intersect it with the plane. The parameter $t$ of the point of intersection also gives you the distance straight away: $d = |t| \cdot |\vec n|$. Combining the calculation gives a formula for which you do not need the foot of the perpendicular at all. In addition, the sign inside the absolute value shows which side of the plane the point lies on.

KEY POINT · DISTANCES

Point and point: $d(P, Q) = |\vec{PQ}| = \sqrt{(q_1 - p_1)^2 + (q_2 - p_2)^2 + (q_3 - p_3)^2}$

Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $E\colon \vec n \circ \vec x = d$: substitute the perpendicular line $\vec x = \vec p + t \cdot \vec n$ into $E$, find $t$, work out $F$.

Distance formula: $d(P, E) = \dfrac{|\vec n \circ \vec p - d|}{|\vec n|}$ · Same sign of $\vec n \circ \vec p - d$: same side of the plane.

Line and plane parallel ($\vec u \circ \vec n = 0$, base point $A$ not in $E$): $d(g, E) = d(A, E)$. Plane and plane parallel: distance of any point of one from the other. If they intersect, the distance is 0.

Hesse normal form (chapter E1.1): if you divide the coordinate equation by $|\vec n|$, i.e. $\tfrac{1}{|\vec n|}(\vec n \circ \vec x - d) = 0$, substituting a point gives its distance with a sign directly.

Parallel planes with the same $\vec n$: $d = \tfrac{|d_1 - d_2|}{|\vec n|}$.

INTERACTIVE · POINTS AND THEIR DISTANCE

Two points, their connecting vector, its length and the midpoint. Dragging rotates the coordinate system.

INTERACTIVE · THE PERPENDICULAR TO THE PLANE

Enter a plane and a point: the widget sets up the perpendicular line, finds the foot of the perpendicular $F$ and the distance in both ways. With the foot of the perpendicular you can also reflect $P$ in the plane: $\vec{OP'} = \vec{OP} + 2\,\vec{PF}$.

EXAMPLE 1 · TWO POINTS

How far apart are $A(2, -1, 3)$ and $B(4, 1, 4)$, and where is the midpoint of the line segment?

$\vec{AB} = (2, 2, 1)$, $|\vec{AB}| = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3$.

$d = 3$, $M(3, 0, 3.5)$

EXAMPLE 2 · FOOT OF THE PERPENDICULAR AND DISTANCE

Find the foot of the perpendicular from $P(4, 3, 2)$ to $E\colon 2x + y + 2z = 6$ and the distance.

Perpendicular line $(4 + 2t, 3 + t, 2 + 2t)$ in $E$: $15 + 9t = 6$, $t = -1$, so $F(2, 2, 0)$.

$d = |t| \cdot |\vec n| = 3$. Check with the formula: $\tfrac{|15 - 6|}{3} = 3$ ✔

EXAMPLE 3 · LINE PARALLEL TO THE PLANE

Show that $g\colon \vec x = (1, 1, 4) + t \cdot (1, 0, -1)$ is parallel to $E\colon 2x + y + 2z = 6$, and find the distance.

$(1, 0, -1) \circ (2, 1, 2) = 2 - 2 = 0$, and $A(1, 1, 4)$ does not lie in $E$ ($2 + 1 + 8 = 11 \ne 6$): parallel.

$d(g, E) = \tfrac{|11 - 6|}{3} = \tfrac53$

FIRST THE POSITION, THEN THE DISTANCE

If a line and a plane or two planes intersect, the distance is 0. So always check $\vec u \circ \vec n$ first, or whether the normal vectors are parallel.

EXERCISES

Calculate the distances: a) $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(3, 4, 4)$   b) $(2, 3, 6)$ from the origin.

a) $\sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3$   b) $\sqrt{49} = 7$

Calculate with the distance formula: a) $O$ from $2x + y + 2z = 6$   b) $(1, 1, 1)$ from $2x - y + 2z = 9$.

a) $\tfrac{6}{3} = 2$   b) $\tfrac{|3 - 9|}{3} = 2$

Which point of the plane $2x + y + 2z = 9$ is nearest to the origin?

Perpendicular line $t \cdot (2, 1, 2)$: $9t = 9$, $t = 1$: $F(2, 1, 2)$, distance 3.

How far apart are the parallel planes $2x + y + 2z = 3$ and $2x + y + 2z = 12$?

$\tfrac{|12 - 3|}{3} = 3$

Calculate the distance between the parallel planes $x - 2y + 2z = 1$ and $x - 2y + 2z = 13$ and the distance from $g\colon \vec x = (0, 0, 2) + t \cdot (2, 1, 0)$ to the first plane.

Planes: $\tfrac{|13 - 1|}{3} = 4$. Line: $(2, 1, 0) \circ (1, -2, 2) = 0$, parallel; $A(0, 0, 2)$: $\tfrac{|4 - 1|}{3} = 1$.

Which points of the $z$-axis are at distance 3 from $E\colon 2x + y + 2z = 6$? On which side of $E$ does each of them lie, compared with the origin?

$\tfrac{|2z - 6|}{3} = 3$: $z = 7.5$ or $z = -1.5$. Sign of $2z - 6$: positive at 7.5 (other side from $O$, which gives −6), negative at −1.5 (same side as $O$).

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Surface areas and volumes of prisms and pyramids

The glass pyramid has the base $A(0, 0, 0)$, $B(4, 0, 0)$, $C(4, 4, 0)$, $D(0, 4, 0)$ and the apex $S(2, 2, 4)$.

Every side face is a triangle. Its area is half the parallelogram spanned by two edge vectors, that is $\tfrac12 |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$. For the volume you only need the base area and the height, as you know from lower secondary school.

KEY POINT · AREAS AND VOLUMES WITH VECTORS

Parallelogram spanned by $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$: $A = |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$ · Triangle: $A = \tfrac12 |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$

Surface area = sum of all faces. Prism: 2 · base area + lateral surface (parallelograms). Pyramid: base area + lateral surface (triangles).

Volume: prism $V = G \cdot h$, pyramid $V = \tfrac13 G \cdot h$. The height $h$ is the perpendicular distance of the apex (or the top face) from the plane of the base, i.e. $h = d(S, E_G)$ as in unit 1.

Cavalieri: an oblique prism has the same volume as a right prism with the same base area and height. The surface area, however, does not.

INTERACTIVE · PYRAMID AND PRISM

Change the base edge and the height and move the apex. Watch what happens to the volume and the lateral surface.

EXAMPLE 4 · THE GLASS PYRAMID

Calculate the lateral surface, the surface area and the volume of the pyramid with $S(2, 2, 4)$.

$\vec{AB} \times \vec{AS} = (4, 0, 0) \times (2, 2, 4) = (0, -16, 8)$, triangle $\tfrac12 \sqrt{320} \approx 8.94$. Lateral surface $4 \cdot 8.94 \approx 35.8$ m². Surface area $\approx 51.8$ m², volume $\tfrac13 \cdot 16 \cdot 4 \approx 21.3$ m³.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE TRIANGULAR PYRAMID

Calculate the volume of the pyramid with $A(0, 0, 0)$, $B(4, 0, 0)$, $C(0, 4, 0)$, $D(0, 0, 4)$.

Base $ABC$ in the $xy$-plane: $\tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 8$, height 4. $V = \tfrac13 \cdot 8 \cdot 4 = \tfrac{32}{3} \approx 10.7$.

EXERCISES

Calculate the area of the triangle $A(1, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 2, 0)$, $C(0, 0, 2)$.

$\vec{AB} = (-1, 2, 0)$, $\vec{AC} = (-1, 0, 2)$, cross product $(4, 2, 2)$, area $\tfrac12 \sqrt{24} \approx 2.45$.

A prism has the base $A(0, 0, 0)$, $B(3, 0, 0)$, $C(0, 4, 0)$ and the top face shifted by $(0, 0, 5)$. Calculate the volume and the surface area.

$G = 6$, $V = 30$. Lateral surface: rectangles $3 \cdot 5$, $4 \cdot 5$, $5 \cdot 5$ (the edge $BC$ is 5 long) $= 60$. $S = 2 \cdot 6 + 60 = 72$.

Show with the widget and explain: if you move the apex of a pyramid parallel to the base, the volume stays the same and the lateral surface gets larger.

The base area and the height do not change, so neither does $V = \tfrac13 G h$. The side faces become more slanted, some triangles clearly larger: the lateral surface is minimal when the apex is above the centre.

FOR THE ADVANCED COURSE · SLANTED BASE

The pyramid has the base $A(4, 0, 0)$, $B(0, 3, 0)$, $C(0, 0, 2)$ and the apex $S(4, 3, 2)$. Calculate the area of the base, the height and the volume. Check with the pyramid $OABC$ with the origin as its apex: what do you notice?

$\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ gives the area and the normal vector, the height is $d(S, E)$ with the Hesse normal form.

$\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = (-4, 3, 0) \times (-4, 0, 2) = (6, 8, 12)$, $G = \tfrac12 \sqrt{244} \approx 7.81$. Plane $3x + 4y + 6z = 12$, $|\vec n| = \sqrt{61}$.

$h = \tfrac{|12 + 12 + 12 - 12|}{\sqrt{61}} = \tfrac{24}{\sqrt{61}} \approx 3.07$, $V = \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt{244}}{2} \cdot \tfrac{24}{\sqrt{61}} = \tfrac{24 \cdot 2\sqrt{61}}{6\sqrt{61}} = $ 8.

With the origin as the apex: base $OAB$ in the $xy$-plane ($\tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 6$), height 2, $V = 4$. $S$ is twice as far from $E$ as $O$ (24 against 12 in the numerator), so twice the volume.

TEST YOURSELF!

Volume of the glass pyramid (base edge 4, height 4)?

$\tfrac{64}{3} \approx 21.33$

Volume of the prism with $G = 6$ and $h = 5$?

30

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

At what angle does a side face of the glass pyramid stand to the base?

Normal vector of the face $ABS$: $(0, -16, 8) \parallel (0, -2, 1)$, base $(0, 0, 1)$: $\cos \varphi = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$, $\varphi \approx 63.4°$.

A radio antenna stands at the point $P(10, 5, 20)$ (in m). A slope is described by $E\colon x + 2y + 2z = 30$. How far is the antenna from the slope, and where is the nearest point of the slope?

$\tfrac{|10 + 10 + 40 - 30|}{3} = 10$ m. Perpendicular line $(10 + t, 5 + 2t, 20 + 2t)$: $60 + 9t = 30$, $t = -\tfrac{10}{3}$: $F\left(\tfrac{20}{3}, -\tfrac53, \tfrac{40}{3}\right)$.

Connecting with chapter 3.4: use the principle “area times thickness” to explain why a pyramid has $\tfrac13$ of the prism. A cross-section at height $z$ has the area $G \cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{z}{h}\right)^2$.

$V = \int_0^h G\left(1 - \tfrac{z}{h}\right)^2 \mathrm{d}z = G \cdot \Big[-\tfrac{h}{3}\left(1 - \tfrac{z}{h}\right)^3\Big]_0^h = \tfrac13 G h$.

EXCURSIONVOLUME 3,800 YEARS AGO

The Moscow Papyrus

In the Pushkin Museum in Moscow there is an Egyptian papyrus from around 1850 BC. Problem 14 calculates the volume of a frustum of a pyramid: a pyramid whose top has been cut off horizontally. At the bottom the square is 4 cubits wide, at the top 2 cubits, the height is 6 cubits.

The scribe calculates: $\tfrac63 \cdot (4^2 + 4 \cdot 2 + 2^2) = 2 \cdot 28 = 56$. That is exactly today's formula $V = \tfrac{h}{3}\left(a^2 + ab + b^2\right)$. How the Egyptians arrived at it, we do not know. With the integral from chapter 3.4 you can prove it today.

Source: Moscow Mathematical Papyrus, problem 14 (around 1850 BC), Pushkin Museum, Moscow.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

FOOT OF THE PERPENDICULAR

Substitute the perpendicular line $\vec p + t\,\vec n$ into $E$.

$P(4, 3, 2)$, $2x + y + 2z = 6$: $F(2, 2, 0)$

DISTANCES TO PLANES

$d(P, E) = \tfrac{|\vec n \circ \vec p - d|}{|\vec n|}$; parallel line or plane: take one point.

$d = 3$ · parallel planes: $\tfrac{|d_1 - d_2|}{|\vec n|}$

AREAS

Parallelogram $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$, triangle $\tfrac12 |\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$

Glass pyramid: lateral surface $\approx 35.8$ m²

VOLUME

Prism $Gh$, pyramid $\tfrac13 Gh$

$\tfrac{64}{3}$ · papyrus: 56
